title: VRAM entropy sleuth - session notes
content:
High-level: intermittent OOMs on a small batch workload (batch_size=1) on p4d nodes. Not reproducing consistently; seems correlated with long-lived process + repeated short sequences (seq_len varying 8-2048). Notes and experiments from pairing session with Diego and Maya.

Summary of symptoms:
- torch app crashes after 1000-4000 requests with CUDA allocation failures.
- error appears as CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED or CUDNN_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED or cudaErrorMemoryAllocation in Python stack.
- nvidia-smi often reports free memory ~200-300 MiB left before apparent crash.
- host OOM killer not triggered; only GPU allocation errors.
- restarting process frees GPU memory and app runs again.

Hypothesis threads (unordered):
1) Fragmentation of device heap due to mixed small/large allocations across kernels. Repeated short sequences cause many cached allocations not reusable due to alignment.
2) Leaky allocator path in a third-party lib (custom kernel op) that holds onto tensors in C++ side; Python-level del() doesn't drop underlying handles.
3) NVML driver bug with stale mappings after many context switches; allocation accounting drifts.
4) mixed CUDA context usage (creating CUDA contexts from both main process and a subprocess/worker) causing memory not fully reclaimed.

Commands & quick checks tried:
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,memory.total,memory.used,memory.free,driver_version --format=csv -l 2 (monitor during run)
- python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.memory_summary(device=0, abbreviated=False))" (snapshots before/after a mini-batch loop)
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u (for utilization trends)
- cat /proc/$(pgrep -f my_app)/status | egrep -i 'VmPeak|VmSize' (to confirm host RSS not growing)
- nvprof / nv-nsight not stable on these nodes; used nvidia-smi & nvmlReader sample script to poll processes.
- docker run --gpus=all --rm -it --ipc=host --env PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 ... to test caching disabled (env var = hypothetical; used TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF instead).

Repro minimal (python snippet) used to trigger quickly:
- loop: call model.generate with random prompts of len 16 - 1024, no gradient, keep warming up for 200 iterations then send 2-4 short inference calls per second. After ~300-1500 iterations it fails.
- Reproducer script used torch 2.1, cuda 12.1, cudnn 8.9, but issue also seen on cuda 11.8 nodes.

Notable error snippets captured:
- RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.25 GiB (GPU 0; 31.75 GiB total capacity; 28.80 GiB already allocated; 512.00 MiB free; 29.00 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)
- CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED when calling cublasCreate_v2
- CUDNN_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR: resource exhaustion at conv_forward_impl
- cudaMalloc returned error: invalid memory allocation (or sometimes unspecified launch failure)

What we observed in memory_summary dumps:
- large reserved pool reported (by default caching allocator) but free_cached sometimes shows hundreds of MiB not used; however allocations fail for contiguous large buffer.
- fragmentation patterns: many small allocations left in active_nbytes with high peak.

Experiments and outcomes:
1) Clear cache between requests: torch.cuda.empty_cache() after each request -> reduces frequency but not eliminating failures.
2) Run with TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:16 -> temporarily improved run-time, fewer OOMs (indicates fragmentation factor).
3) Force GPU memory defag (not possible directly) but restarting process cleans state -> deterministic recovery.
4) Set environment NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to restrict network interfaces -> no impact.
5) Run single-threaded worker (no multiprocessing.spawn) -> fewer races, but still OOM after longer runtime.
6) Upgrade/revert driver: tested driver 535.XX vs 530.XX; both reproduce but thresholds vary (more tolerant on 535).
7) Switched to torch compile vs eager: compiled model had different memory layout and crashed later; not conclusive.
8) Instrumented C++ extension (my-custom-op) with a destructor log; no steady leaks seen in logs but destructor not always called (maybe due to caching).

Driver / sys info snapshot (from one failing node):
- CUDA Version: 12.1
- NVIDIA-SMI 535.86.10   Driver Version: 535.86.10
- GPU: A100-SXM4-80GB (but also seen on p4d with 40GB)
- Kernel: 6.1.0-25
- Docker runtime: nvidia-container-runtime v3, containerd 1.7

dmesg excerpt around crash:
[  1123.123456] device: pci 0000:3b:00.0: BAR 0: memory map failure - continuing, may leak
[  1137.654321] NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus.
(we have seen rare "GPU has fallen off the bus" but mostly not; more common is silent allocation failure)

Notes about third-party libs:
- Using a tokenizer that returns memoryviews that are converted into torch tensors via frombuffer(); ensure they do not own extra memory.
- A custom CUDA kernel lib (libfastop.so) uses its own allocator (cudaMalloc/cudaFree). Could hold fragmentation. Checked C++ code: allocs returned OK and frees called, but no pooling.

Checklist for next steps (prio order):
- [ ] Add detailed periodic dumps of torch.cuda.memory_allocated() and torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() with timestamps to correlate with request ids.
- [ ] Instrument libfastop to add allocation counters and callstack logging for allocations > 1MB (use backtrace).
- [ ] Re-run with TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:8 on a stable node for 24h to see regression.
- [ ] Try using pybind11-based weakref hooks to ensure CPU->GPU tensor views drop references promptly.
- [ ] Spin up a controlled experiment with only two sequence lengths (16 and 2048) to maximize fragmentation contrast.
- [ ] File driver debug ticket with NV support including memory snapshots & process vmmap from /proc/<pid>/smaps (NV support asked for "nvidia-debugdump" dump).

Low-probability wild ideas (to record):
- Page migration bug between GPUs when nvlink is present can create orphaned DMA regions. Check nvlink topology and test with NVLINK disabled if possible.
- Kernel config in our AMI changed malloc behavior after recent kernel bump; check glibc version and jemalloc usage in stack.

Ephemeral breadcrumbs (things to remember):
- When reproduction fails, try leaving process idle for 30s and then triggering a large allocation; sometimes crash only after sustained activity.
- Use a separate control process that polls nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo via python-nvml to capture near-failure state.
- Slack thread: infra-gpu #F12345 has console logs from 2025-02-11 run.

Notes to self: this doc is a scratchpad. Add stack traces raw and small test harness later. Keep trying to reduce variables: single lib version, single CUDA, single driver. If fragmentation remains likely, try explicit allocation-churn mitigations (pre-allocating large pool, reuse buffers keyed by size).

Reference commands to copy into a debug-run script:
- python -u run_repro.py --batch 1 --warmup 200 --loop 4000 2>&1 | tee repro-$(date +%s).log
- env TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:16 python -u run_repro.py
- python -c 'import pynvml; pynvml.nvmlInit(); h=pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0); print(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo(h))'

Last observed concrete lead: setting max_split_size_mb to 16 pushed crash window out by ~3x consistently across 3 nodes. That points at fragmentation being a large contributor. Next lock-step: instrument allocation sizes and try small max_split (8 or 4) to see effect.

-- Aisha
